narrative: During the 1940s, Black and African women's hairstyles and hair culture were deeply rooted in tradition and identity. While the specific details of hairstyles during this era are scarce, we can infer from the existing information that protective styles such as cornrows and Bantu knots would have been popular among women with afro-textured hair. These styles not only reduced breakage but also celebrated the natural texture of their hair. The Jheri curl, a permanent wave hairstyle, was not introduced until the 1980s, so it is unlikely to have been worn during this decade. However, African-American culture and its emphasis on collective struggle for civil rights would have played a significant role in shaping the way women wore their hair as an expression of identity and community. Unfortunately, due to limited documentation from this era, we cannot provide a more detailed account of hairstyles and hair culture specific to the 1940s.
